title: Lesson 2
subtitle: Working with a Topic — Which one?
objectives: Mark the topic of a sentence with the particle wa
Choose between dore (three or more items) and docchi (two items)
Memorize the ko so a do pattern: kore, sore, are, dore and kocchi, socchi, acchi, docchi
Use the new phrases for talking about speaking a language
Know the difference between sushi and sashimi
Read and write hiragana か き く け こ plus the dakuten versions が ぎ ぐ げ ご

vocab.japanese: にほんごがはなせますか
えいごがはなせますか
にほんごをべんきょうしています

grammar.title: The topic marker wa
grammar.explanation: The particle wa marks the topic of the sentence. It can be thought to mean 'Speaking of (the) ~' or 'As for (the) ~', but it does not have any meaning in English. Everything that comes before wa is the topic or part of the topic; everything after wa describes or asks a question about the topic.

examples.japanese: あしたはげつようびです。
ゆかりさんはにほんじんです。

mistakes: Treating wa as a word with English meaning — it only marks the topic

grammar.title: Cool Tools: the ko so a do pattern
grammar.pattern: ko- = close, so- = sort of close, a- = in the distance, do- = question word
grammar.explanation: Japanese has word groups that follow the ko so a do pattern. This lesson has two: kore, sore, are, dore and kocchi, socchi, acchi, docchi. ko means close enough to touch; so means sort of close, but not enough to touch; a means in the distance, definitely not close; do is the question word.

examples.japanese: これ・それ・あれ・どれ
examples.english: this one / that one / that one over there / which one

examples.japanese: こっち・そっち・あっち・どっち
examples.english: this one / that one / that one over there / which one (two items)

mistakes: Mixing up the four similar-sounding words in a ko-so-a-do group — remember the distance diagram

grammar.title: The question words dore and docchi
grammar.pattern: [topic] + wa dore desu ka / [topic] + wa docchi desu ka
grammar.explanation: Dore and docchi both mean 'which one?'. Dore is used with groups of three or more; if there are only two items, docchi is used.

examples.english: Which one is the car? (three or more)

examples.japanese: やさいはどっちですか。
examples.english: Which one is the vegetable? (two items)

mistakes: Using docchi for a group of three or more — that needs dore

grammar.title: Following the same pattern when answering
grammar.pattern: answer with the same sentence shape as the question
grammar.explanation: The answers and questions in the example Q&A follow the same sentence pattern. When answering questions, remember that 90% of the answer is in the question. Also, when the question has ~cchi in it, the answer should not change to ~re — keep response sentences in the same format as their question sentences.

examples.japanese: かがみはどれですか。かがみはそれです。
examples.romaji: Kagami wa dore desu ka. / Kagami wa sore desu.
examples.english: Which one is a mirror? / That one is a mirror.

examples.japanese: まどはどっちですか。まどはあっちです。
examples.romaji: Mado wa docchi desu ka. / Mado wa acchi desu.
examples.english: Which one is a window? / That one over there is a window.

mistakes: Answering a ~cchi question with a ~re word

grammar.title: Using what you know to learn more
grammar.pattern: [word] wa nan desu ka / [word] wa [answer] desu
grammar.explanation: If you don't know a word, use the Japanese you know to ask someone what the word is. For example, if you don't know what enpitsu means, ask 'Enpitsu wa nan desu ka?' — the answer comes back in the same shape: 'Enpitsu wa pencil desu.'

examples.japanese: えんぴつはなんですか。
えんぴつはペンシルです。

mistakes: Switching to English to ask what a word means when you can ask in Japanese

grammar.title: Speaking Naturally: dropping the topic
grammar.pattern: state the topic once, then use 'incomplete' sentences
grammar.explanation: It's very common in Japanese to drop the topic of a conversation once it has been introduced. In English we constantly restate the topic directly or use 'he', 'she', 'they'. Spoken Japanese is much more like a match of tennis: a topic is served and then discussed back and forth, and it is not mentioned again until a new topic is served. What would be incomplete sentences in English are natural in Japanese.

examples.japanese: わたしのともだちはみちこさんです。
examples.romaji: Watashi no tomodachi wa Michiko san desu.

examples.japanese: にほんにすんでいます。

mistakes: Repeating the topic (or 'she') in every sentence the way English does

grammar.title: Culture Clip: Sushi and Sashimi
grammar.pattern: sushi = fish (or eggs / vegetables) on rice; sashimi = sliced raw fish
grammar.explanation: Many foreigners to Japan don't know the difference between sushi and sashimi. Sushi is raw or cooked fish, eggs, or vegetables on rice, placed on top of a fist-full of rice, and normally there is some wasabi between the fish and rice. Wasabi is a Japanese horseradish; it is very pungent. Sashimi is just sliced raw fish.
mistakes: Calling sliced raw fish without rice 'sushi'

grammar.title: Hiragana か き く け こ and the dakuten
grammar.pattern: ka = か, ki = き, ku = く, ke = け, ko = こ; dakuten turns them into ga gi gu ge go
grammar.explanation: The new hiragana are か き く け こ. Adding the dakuten (two small strokes up in the right hand corner) to か き く け こ makes が ぎ ぐ げ ご. When adding dakuten to か, make sure the strokes are shorter than the third stroke of が. There are two versions of き: a four-stroke version that is very common in handwriting, and a version with the third and fourth strokes combined into one that is common in printed text. Both are used in Japan.

examples.english: key — か plus ぎ (dakuten on き)

mistakes: Making the dakuten on が longer than its third stroke

quiz.explanation: Everything before wa is the topic; everything after wa describes or asks about the topic.

summary: Wa marks the topic: everything before wa is the topic, everything after describes or asks about it ([topic] + wa + [question or description]). The ko so a do pattern gives two groups this lesson — kore / sore / are / dore and kocchi / socchi / acchi / docchi — with dore for three or more items and docchi for two. Keep answers in the same pattern as their questions, and drop the topic once it has been introduced. New phrases cover speaking languages (Sukoshi = a little, Zenzen = not at all). New hiragana: か き く け こ plus dakuten versions が ぎ ぐ げ ご.
